subject: Science
title: The shapes of Sun, Earth and Moon
objective_verbatim: Describe the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies.
reading_age_est: rough ARI grade 3.63 on 862 pupil-visible words; heuristic age guide 9.63 years, not a formal reading-age test
pupil_words: show how a ball models the Sun, Earth and Moon.
success_criteria: I can choose a ball to model a round body.
I can turn it to show more than one side.
I can name one limit of a model.

vocab.definition: a line or surface that bends
vocab.example: The ball has a curved surface.

vocab.definition: a dark area where an object blocks light
vocab.example: The ball makes a shadow on the card.

vocab.definition: a simple way to show an object or idea
vocab.example: A ball is a model of Earth’s shape.

retrieval.question: What makes day turn to night at one place?
Name one force you have explored.

stages.pupil_text: Sort a coin, paper circle and ball: flat or solid?
stages.adult_text: Offer a predictable seat or standing spot and the first visual cue. No public test.

stages.pupil_text: Think back. Say, point or write one answer for each question.
stages.adult_text: Ask three low-stakes retrieval questions; prior coverage must be checked.

stages.pupil_text: Watch me turn a ball. I can see another curved side. A paper circle is flat. A ball helps show the shape of the Sun, Earth and Moon, but its size is not exact.
stages.adult_text: Model the full reasoning step, pre-teach four words and ask the show-me question.

stages.pupil_text: Use a ball and a paper circle. The model and first label are ready. Turn the ball and complete the missing label: new side or the same flat face?
stages.adult_text: Show the part-done example, then allow paired talk before an answer. One-minute reset inside this stage.

stages.pupil_text: Show everyone which shape model lets us turn to see another side.
stages.adult_text: All pupils answer the four-option hinge; use the decision rule, not a score.

stages.pupil_text: Turn a shape model. Explain one way it helps and one limit. You can show, say or draw.
stages.adult_text: One adult supports agreed pupils, the other holds the group; swap across the week. One-minute reset inside this stage.

stages.pupil_text: Hear a comment on your model. Change one label or spoken reason and say what changed.
stages.adult_text: Give a specific verbal comment (VF) and invite one self-edit (//) or read-back (?).

stages.pupil_text: Show which shape model helps. Say one way it helps and one thing it cannot show exactly.
stages.adult_text: Hear the answer and name how it changes the next example or support. One-minute reset and handoff.

worked_example.full: Ball → turn it → see another curved side → useful for an approximately spherical body; ball sizes and gaps are not to scale.
worked_example.faded: Ball → turn it → see ____ → useful because ____.
worked_example.removed_step: Name the new curved side and explain why it helps.
worked_example.fade_next: Next time remove the ball cue and ask for a model choice before showing kit.

cfu.question: Point: which object can I turn to see another curved side?

hinge.question: A class models the Moon’s whole shape. Which object is the closest simple shape?

options.diagnosis: Uses a flat circle for a three-dimensional Moon.
Mistakes a long one-dimensional shape for a round body.
Chooses a flat square because the diagram is on paper.

hinge.decision_rule: About 3 in 4 or more right → move on. Otherwise re-model with the named I-do example, then ask the parallel hinge.
hinge.parallel_hinge: Which simple shape could model the Sun’s whole shape: ball or flat ring? Answer: ball; neither size nor gaps are to scale.

misconceptions.misconception: A circle on paper is a sphere.
misconceptions.spot: Pupil chooses A, “A thin flat disc.”
misconceptions.correction: Turn a ball to reveal a new side; a flat circle cannot do that.

misconceptions.misconception: Spherical means perfectly smooth and exactly round.
misconceptions.spot: Pupil describes C as perfectly smooth and exactly round.
misconceptions.correction: Say approximately spherical; the real bodies are not exact toy balls.

we_do.support: Point to the ball and the paper edge before you turn the model.
we_do.stretch: Explain why one photo can look circular but cannot show the full solid shape.
we_do.F: Point to the ball and the paper edge before you turn the model.
we_do.M: Turn the ball and explain what new view it gives.
we_do.H: Explain why one photo can look circular but cannot show the full solid shape.

tiers.F: Choose a ball rather than a flat circle.
tiers.M: Turn the ball and explain what new view it gives.
tiers.H: Explain what a ball model reveals and how its scale may mislead.

stems.F: I choose the ___ to show shape.
stems.M: When I turn it, I see ___ because ___.
stems.H: The model helps because ___; its limit is ___.

tiers.go_deeper: Compare a ball and a photo. What can each show, and what does each hide?
tiers.early_finisher: A photo shows Earth as a circle. Choose another observation or model to test its full shape. Explain why one photo is not enough.

adaptations.cognition_learning: Give a tactile ball and a two-step turn card, then remove the turn cue.
adaptations.communication_interaction: Let pupils rehearse the M or H model explanation with a partner and pointing cue.
adaptations.semh: Offer a safe kit role and quiet pause cue before the model comparison.
adaptations.sensory_physical: Use a large stable ball or textured ball; allow a photo of the pupil’s real demonstration.
adaptations.eal: Teach spherical with a ball and gesture. Keep M/H open with the speaking frame and home-language planning.

speaking_frames: When I turn it, I see ___ because ___.
The model helps because ___; its limit is ___.

ta_focus.i_do: Watch the ball, then point to the side you can see.
ta_focus.we_do: What is done? What does turning show next?
ta_focus.independent: Show your model choice. What can you explain yourself?

prompt_ladder: Point to the lesson’s diagram, kit or source.
Ask: What is done, and what is the next step?
Model one step, then return the next step to the pupil.
Finish one example together, then fade the help.

M.q: What changes when you turn the ball?
Why is the ball a useful shape model?
M.a: It has a curved surface on more than one side.

H.q: What is one limit of the toy-ball model?
H.a: Its size, texture or distance may not match the real body.

H.q: Why is one flat photo not enough?
H.a: It only shows one view of a solid body.

interactions.answer_key: Ball labels the approximately spherical model; paper circle is flat.

diagrams.alt: A flat disc is shown face-on and edge-on beside a shaded solid sphere shown before and after turning; another curved side comes into view.
diagrams.caption: The disc is flat. A ball has a curved surface even when turned. Simplified shape model; not to scale.

practical.prediction: Predict which object can turn to show a different curved side: ball or paper circle?
kit: Three safe balls or modelling spheres
method: Compare a ball with a flat circle.
Turn the ball once and record what new side you see.
Turn the paper circle and record what it shows.
Put the torch on the ball; do not point it into eyes.
results_table: Shape model | new curved side seen?
practical.risk: Check against the school risk assessment and CLEAPSS guidance. Keep the torch beam out of eyes; use safe, stable kit.
practical.pupil_risk: Torch beams can dazzle eyes; round models may roll off the table.
practical.pupil_safety: Keep the beam out of eyes. Turn models over the tray and put them back.

facts.claim: The Sun is roughly round rather than a flat circle.
facts.source: NASA Science, Sketch the Shape of the Sun, https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/skywatching/sketch-the-shape-of-the-sun-for-science-during-the-solar-eclipse/

facts.claim: The Moon is an imperfect sphere.
A simple ball model can show a solid body’s curved surface but does not represent every feature or scale.
facts.source: NASA eClips Glossary, model/simulation, https://science.nasa.gov/eclips/resources/glossary/; NASA Science, What is a Planet?, https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/what-is-a-planet/

facts.claim: A flat paper circle has only a flat surface; turning a ball reveals another curved side.
An object blocks light to make a shadow.
Earlier rows teach Earth’s rotation, planetary movement and forces.

stages: Arrival (5 min): Sort a coin, paper circle and ball: flat or solid? Staff: Offer a predictable seat or standing spot and the first visual cue. No public test.
Starter (3 min): Think back. Say, point or write one answer for each question. Staff: Ask three low-stakes retrieval questions; prior coverage must be checked.

I Do (5 min): Watch me turn a ball. I can see another curved side. A paper circle is flat. A ball helps show the shape of the Sun, Earth and Moon, but its size is not exact. Staff: Model the full reasoning step, pre-teach four words and ask the show-me question.

We Do (7 min): Use a ball and a paper circle. The model and first label are ready. Turn the ball and complete the missing label: new side or the same flat face? Staff: Show the part-done example, then allow paired talk before an answer. One-minute reset inside this stage.
We Do 2 (5 min): Show everyone which shape model lets us turn to see another side. Staff: All pupils answer the four-option hinge; use the decision rule, not a score.

Independent (8 min): Turn a shape model. Explain one way it helps and one limit. You can show, say or draw. Staff: One adult supports agreed pupils, the other holds the group; swap across the week. One-minute reset inside this stage.
Review (4 min): Hear a comment on your model. Change one label or spoken reason and say what changed. Staff: Give a specific verbal comment (VF) and invite one self-edit (//) or read-back (?).

Exit (3 min): Show which shape model helps. Say one way it helps and one thing it cannot show exactly. Staff: Hear the answer and name how it changes the next example or support. One-minute reset and handoff.
